newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parliament debates opening police files.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parliament debates opening police files.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament took a step on Friday towards allowing communist-era police files to be opened to prevent attempts to blackmail politicians.

"This law will enable us join the European Union without the threat of manipulations...it will also help us combat organised crime," Prime Minister Ivan Kostov told the assembly which gave preliminary approval to the bill on Friday.

Opening the files was a major plank of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) manifesto for April elections, but its opponents warn too much time has passed and the files could be a Pandora's Box for the new government.
"The opening of the files will end possibilities to blackmail people who were formerly associated with the former state security service," said Justice Minister Vassil Gotsev.
Under the draft law approved by the UDF cabinet 10 days ago, the files of members of parliament, ministers, senior government officials and high-ranking judges will be opened.
The law will now go back to the parliamentary commissions and will be returned to parliament for a second reading in two weeks.

Kostov urged deputies to consider adding clauses to the law to protect existing agents working for the security service. He also urged them to consider expanding the circle of officials whose files should be opened.
The Kontinent daily newspaper said on Friday it estimated that around 50 of parliament's 240 deputies were associated in one way or another with the former secret police.
Several prominent UDF figures, including former leaders Filip Dimitrov and Petar Beron, have been accused of having cooperated with the security services.

A former intelligence officer said last month that Ahmed Dogan, leader of the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms and chairman of a coalition which forms the third biggest bloc in parliament, had been recruited when he was a student.
"The opening of the files will put an end to the war of compromising materials," said Gotsev. "It will also unveil essential information from our recent history."
Reformist President Petar Stoyanov said on Thursday he would insist on having his file opened.

The State Security Service was dissolved in 1989 and its files are kept by the interior and defence ministries, the National Intelligence Service and the National Protection Service, which assures security for public figures.
The agencies would be required to submit the relevant files to the prime minister a month after the law was passed.
Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said in April he felt it was now too late to open the files because he believed they had been tampered with.
More than seven years since the end of one-party rule have provided ample opportunity for records to be forged, substituted or destroyed, critics of the draft law believe.
Bulgaria's communist secret service, closely allied to the Soviet KGB, had a network of 100,000 agents and informers.

Opening secret police files has been a controversial step even in former East Germany, although made easier by the clean break the former communist state made with the past by unifying with West Germany and disbanding its own intelligence service.
